JRPGs often get bogged down in unnecessary complexity and padding, Shadows of Adam stands out as a beacon of concise and engaging storytelling. This retro-style gem is a testament to the power of focused game design, delivering a narrative that is both emotionally resonant and expertly paced. From the moment you start playing. 

Every scene, every conversation, and every plot twist serves a purpose, propelling the story forward with a sense of urgency and momentum.

The game's combat system is turn-based and strategic, with a unique AP system that rewards careful planning and execution. Battles are challenging but never feel overwhelming, and the sense of satisfaction you get from developing strats for bosses is great! 

There is not any excessive exposition or tedious backtracking. The game's world is meticulously crafted, with a clear sense of history and lore that feeds the narrative. No fetch quests for the sake of time padding, no "oh he's in the OTHER castle" bull, just good proper story and gameplay.

Shadows of Adam begins unassumingly enough. Kellen and his adoptive sister Astrael are traveling through a region of forest near their town, the titular Adam, that has become wildly overgrown with carnivorous flora. What they discover there sends them off into the world on adventure to find out what happened to Kellen’s father and ultimately save the world from the revivification of a magical artifact called the wraith crystal.

The gameplay in Shadows of Adam will be thoroughly familiar to fans of the genre. Characters have hit points and skill points, they learn new abilities as they level up, and they take turns using their selected actions in battle. However, there are few interesting nuances. Most notably is that skill points are expressed exclusively as a percentage, and while there are a handful of items and effects that can allow the percentage to rise above 100, generally the characters all start and end the game with the same max skill pool throughout. As a result of this change, managing my skill point balance and strategically planning for battles was indeed much more interesting. The skills themselves are also interesting and unique in their own right and remain useful throughout the game.

The graphics are done in a style reminiscent of early nineties RPGs, such as Final Fantasy 4, Secret of Mana, etc. The art style is visually appealing while fitting the retro aesthetic. The same can be said for the music, all of which is expertly scored.

It took me 13 hours to complete this game. However, I expect many players will do it more quickly, since I tend to take my time exploring everything and grinding out levels. This brings me to my one critique of the game. While I find the story expertly crafted, all of a piece, nothing extraneous, and coherent throughout, I find myself vaguely wanting more of it. It would have been nice to explore some of the characters' backstories more thoroughly, or to create situations where the characters delve into their time before the game’s story picks up properly–“Shadows of Adam” is an apt name, as much of the depth is derived from how the game’s backstory affects the character relationships in the here-and-now of the narrative.

This was a thoroughly satisfying title, and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes turn-based RPGs, particularly if you like the 90’s aesthetic.

(   Don't buy this game is has a portal reference in it >:[   )

If you are looking for a final fantasy 1 esc RPG that isn't a parody of the JRPG genre, then you will have an enjoyable time with this game. It's linear, and ~10 hours long, but I enjoyed my time.

[h1]----Summary[/h1]
Shadows of Adam is a classical NES/Master System styled JRPG. It is very similar in style to Final Fantasy 1-5 in looks, but the battle system is more refined. I know this sounds weird, but it is more of a take on the modern "RPGmaker" default combat system, but not a carbon copy. It is extremely refined with enough spells spread across the 4 characters you control to give you enough variety in how you chose to play. You can more or less pick anyone as your main damage dealer and come out ok for the whole game.


[h1]----Positives[/h1]
[h3]Nice Classic Graphics[/h3]
It is very clear that this game was going for a final fantasy 1-5 kind of feel with the graphics and it nails it without being too similar. It doesn't look like they traced over Final Fantasy 4 sprites. It also doesn't have extremely tiny graphics that are 1 pixel big.

The battle sprites for the enemies look really great, and remind me a lot of DOS games with EGA or VGA graphics, though this has way more colors than EGA. Overall its a very charming game if you like the classic Final Fantasy's (Pre PlayStaion)

[h3]Turn Based Battle System is Good[/h3]
For its simplicity, the battle system is very good. Each character has a wide variety of abilities that make all of the characters you get useful. You will need to change strategies based on the combo of monsters you are fighting, and the battles are pretty fast. You won't be wasting time grinding monsters with your basic attack.

The mana system has you refunding a small amount mana every turn, so you are encouraged to use your abilities to get things done. There is also an ability on each character that restores more mana and provides another benefit without providing damage that turn. Every move you make furthers your goal of winning, so it never feels like you are wasting a turn.

[h3]Doesn't Overstay Its Welcome[/h3]
I for one am happy this game took ~10 hours instead of 20. I don't like it when games waste my time with long annoying puzzles, forcing me to grind to beat a boss, or have an annoying encounter rate.

Battles are started by running into monsters on the overworld. You will be forced to fight several, but only when you are ready for them. You get quite a bit of XP when you finish a battle too, so you don't need to do all the optional ones if you are good at the battle system, or use items. You can save anywhere, which is always nice.

Finally, no random encounters means doing the puzzles are lot less frustrating, and the puzzles themselves are designed to keep you moving. 

No fat in this game.


[h1]----Negatives[/h1]
[h3]Characters Are a Bit Shallow[/h3]
If you are expecting nuanced characters like you would get in a more modern RPG, this game is not for you. The characters are pretty simple, and their dialog is a little stiff. You get the feeling they all know each other, mostly, but their interactions can be grating. Not the most well written RPG, though I played it for the plot, not the characters. This game is at its best when the plot is happening.

Final Fantasy 1 didn't even have interactions between the characters, so I guess this is in upgrade technically.

[h3]Weird Graphical "Breathing Effect" On My Screen[/h3]
I tried lots of different things to fix it, but whether full screen or windowed, the game would "breath". That is to say, then entire game would scale up and down ever so slightly all the time, giving my screen a weird "shimmer" or "breathing" effect and no graphics options changed it. It was really only noticeable when I wasn't moving my character, but I can't imagine it was good for my eyes.

Not sure what was up with this.

[h3]The Portal Reference[/h3]
I was willing to give you a pass with the blatant Rydia reference because the entire game is wearing its reference on its sleeve pretty tastefully, and it was in an optional area technically, but the cake joke? Come on dude. Those jokes weren't even funny when portal came out.

Us gamers am I right?


[h1]----Conclusion[/h1]
This is a very fun little game, especially if you like turn based RPGs. There isn't a grand story, or lots of side quests, but for what it is, I enjoyed it and think it is very well made.

You could spend an afternoon with a worse game.

Shadows of Adam is not a bad game by any means, it just doesn't really have anything going for it. Art style is nice, music ranges from decent and forgettable to good and forgettable, and the battle system is fine (though the blazing fast battles disclaimer isn't exactly it). Your characters have about 8 to 10 skills, but for the most part you'll only use a couple per character (for example, main character Kellan's single target damage doesn't really compare to just using his turn to buff AoE spellcaster Azrael) and you regenerate 15% AP per turn. Dungeons thus become managing your health and your AP so that you always have enough to tackle the next (static) encounter. It's different and nice enough.

Dialogue is pretty bad. The great majority of the story is delivered through five to seven-word long sentences and makes for pretty horrible reading honestly. When your characters interact with one another, it's to make fun of each other, very rarely to discuss their objectives or their current situation. The entirety of the party's motivations are delivered through the dozen or so flashbacks spread throughout the game but even then, they aren't interesting in the slightest. There's some backstory about the Wraith War and the origin of magic but frankly it's whatever. One of the antagonists is some blatant attempt at making a Kefka Palazzo but without the wits or the competence that made him threatening. And the other antagonist uhhhhh is pretty blatant but the party is too dumb/don't talk between themselves to discuss so it's supposed to come as a surprise but really isn't.

Another big sore point for me is the recycling of the same puzzles over and over. The first dungeons start off nice enough, but then they introduce the Orb-pushing puzzle (self-explanatory, push an orb around statues/objects to push it into a hole) and the Minecart puzzle (flip switches, go on the right track) which are used constantly until the end of the game after their first appearance. As a big fan of old-school RPGs like FF6, I had a lot of fun with this game. Overworld traversal is like Final Fantasy Mystic Quest (enemies stand on the field, no random battles, yay!) but the battles are much more interesting to play and the story is more developed than Mystic Quest. It's also quite fast-paced, battles last just the perfect amount of time to allow time to facilitate various strategies without feeling like a drag. Many modern RPG's have battles that last too long for my taste, so this a big plus for me.

Gameplay in general is great! It's fun to link together different combinations of abilities and be creative. My favorite thing is to go for all the buffs and massive damage on one character! For equipment, you get a weapon, an armor and an accessory per character. You may be thinking "Just one accessory?". Enter Grand Reliquaries, which once found will allow you to combine three accessories into one for each character. These are REALLY fun to play with because of how good some of the accessories are. Synergizing them together in different combinations lets you flex your creative muscle. Best of all, there's a super challenging end-game optional dungeon to test your mettle once you've found your favorite strategies. The gameplay's weak point is the puzzles. Most of them involve pushing objects to get to a destination. It works, but the difficulty ramp feels a little steep on them at times and they are used too often so they lose their charm after a while (That said I actually enjoyed the stealth minigame, heh). You will likely need a guide for the puzzles in the optional dungeon!

As for the story, it's solid. It's not as developed as the gameplay, but what's there works well enough. And there were moments which were really great like when you're sneaking through a certain town. It's also a game with story flashbacks that were actually quite short, interesting, and enjoyable, which is a rare sight! The character dynamic isn't always perfect, for example once you get all four characters, there's two main characters who bicker with each other to the point that it slows the pace of the story. There are a few bad guys (one of which will immediately remind you of Kefka), but for each of them they either aren't there enough, or they aren't enough of threat. So unfortunately something is missing in the villain department, and I do consider that a really important aspect of any RPG.

That said, if it was a longer game, I could see the story flaws becoming a bigger issue, but the story is still more than good enough to justify the game's length when combined with the great gameplay. I can safely recommend Shadows of Adam if you are a fan of the great turn-based RPG's of the 90's! And even if you aren't, the battles are short and fun, so there's a good chance you might enjoy it anyways.

This is a love letter to SNES-era RPGs - I was reminded a lot of FF4, FF6 and FFMQ while playing (in fact there are some flat out references!)  I'm a big fan of the genre and not only that, SoA is a high quality game in its own right.

The pixel art is excellent, from the environments, to the sprites, to the animations (there aren't a ton of animations but there's just enough.)

The music is similarly well done; there are several battle themes and a theme for each area of the game.  Many of these evoke memories of analogous locations in Final Fantasy games.

The battle system is simple but tactical.  It's critical to manage your AP level not only in a fight but between fights.  Each character gets a dozen or so techniques over time and these are well balanced so that the advanced techs don't completely obsolete older ones.

Occasionally the game will troll you with surprise battles but for the most part the monsters are visible in the dungeons and you initiate battles by walking up to them (mystic quest / romancing saga style) which I prefer.  

You can save anywhere you want, and if I had to nitpick I would say this makes the game too easy.  This game may take you 10 hours to finish it the first time, but there are optional dungeons and bosses that are rewarding, and the DLC is definitely worth getting - it introduces the reliquaries system which allows you to combine the effects of 3 relics at once, which is necessary to build a killer party.  It took me 40+ hrs to 100% this game, but I completed all the optional areas/bosses during the regular game and New Game + which isn't required.  The juicebox achievement is the most difficult and rewards you for very thoroughly searching towns.  You will have no problems gaining EXP levels - the regular monsters are very generous.  I never felt like I had to grind at any point.  By the time I was trying to get the Level 50 achievement I was almost there anyway.

The story is a mixed bag.  In the beginning it wasn't clear to me how seriously this game takes itself.  There is a lot of slapstick dialogue (3/4 of the main characters are children, after all).  But there are also many serious scenes, usually in flashbacks, and once you figure out what is going on some of the storyline is rather dark.  

The game is really linear for the most part, but once you get the airship the whole map opens up and you can go back to previous areas and to some areas completely inaccessible otherwise.  This was great, but it only happens at the end of the game; you could just drop right into the Abyss and go to the endgame dungeon if you want.  Or you could explore, and there is some fun stuff to find.  A minimap really would have helped for the airship - I got lost a lot trying to find specific islands.

Overall this is a very good retro RPG, I would recommend.

It's a pretty good, simple, modern take on a SNES era JRPG.  Shorter play time (I beat the base game in about 20 hours), smaller cast (only 4 playable, all of whom you get pretty early in the story), more tactical combat than most.  Every character has special moves that cost mana, and compared to JRPGs of the time characters can cast a lot fewer spells before needing to regain some mana.  But they passively get some back every turn, and have abilities (and items) that can gain even more.  It leads to much more consideration of what to do each turn, instead of a lot of JRPGs where the characters just have a best attack they can do every turn and there is no particular thought to what to do.

Some of the dungeon puzzles were fairly difficult, and I would have found them frustrating if there had been random battles interrupting me the whole time, but this game has no random battles.  Instead you can see your enemies standing around before you fight them, which I thought was a smart move.  You can make them respawn by leaving the area and coming back.

The plot was pretty good, and cohesive throughout.  The main character and his rival (also playable) got irritating to me a couple times, but most of the game I liked them.   I appreciated how interwoven everyones plotlines were, with new twists and connections being revealed throughout the entire game.

Overall I would have liked it if the game had been fleshed out like 20% more in several areas, but I definitely enjoyed it.
